title: Cover — The Flats
summary: Sell Chapter 1 through the threshold itself: six old friends are about to leave a functioning Harbor Phase and walk onto exposed seabed toward something barely visible offshore. The cover should make the crossing irresistible without spending the chapter's full district reveal.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed portrait comic-cover image; no interior panel grid and no recap collage.

Primary composition: low, slightly behind the six friends at the floodwall steps as they prepare to leave wet concrete and step onto black exposed seabed. Their headlamps and practical gear form a small human cluster against the floodwall mass and open fog.

The offshore district must NOT be fully revealed. Show only a few enormous geometric hints through fog—perhaps a dark vertical tower edge, a broken elevated line, or distant construction mass—enough to promise scale without giving away the Chapter 1 panoramic reveal.
Harbor Phase remains visibly alive behind/above them through occupied lights, transit glow and practical infrastructure. The choice to cross must feel voluntary, not like escape from dystopia.

Thumbnail read: six small bright practical-light points at the bottom-middle, one strong floodwall/step diagonal, and one ambiguous offshore silhouette. The eye should immediately read THRESHOLD, PEOPLE, UNKNOWN.

Reserve clean atmospheric negative space in the upper quarter and upper-left/upper-center for the established Low Tide Signal masthead/trade dress. Keep the strongest architecture out of the masthead zone.
Palette: rain gray, deep cyan fog, black mud/water, restrained sodium amber and contractor white. No beige wash, no neon, no supernatural glow.
Spoiler ceiling: do not show the full offshore district, Fashion Harbor Center, runner culture, Tide Town social occupation, or anything learned after the first crossing begins.
directionInline: Before generation, retrieve and visually inspect the actual pixels of starsplitterrecords/StarSplitterVisions@main:sites/visions/public/images/covers/low-tide-signal-issue-01-cover.png. Use that image ONLY as cover-trade-dress authority: masthead/logotype shape and placement, title hierarchy, issue/chapter label behavior, recurring brand marks, and overall cover-brand rhythm. Do not use its depicted figures as character-identity authority and do not copy its scene composition.

This recipe controls the new Chapter 1 selling image. The cover must feel like a premium prestige-indie comic someone would pick up at thumbnail size: one dominant idea, strong silhouette hierarchy, disciplined negative space, grounded coastal science fiction, and no generic cast-lineup posing.
Do not invent blurbs, prices, barcodes, credits, logos, environmental promotional text, or decorative labels not established by the approved cover-trade-dress reference or explicitly scripted here.

title: Cover — The Dead Mall
summary: Sell Chapter 2 through the contradiction that makes the offshore district addictive: a mall that should be dead is becoming a temporary human place. The flooded architecture should be majestic and wrong; the people above the water should make it feel occupied rather than haunted.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed portrait comic-cover image; one dominant atrium composition, not a montage.

Camera from an upper mall level looking diagonally across a vast salt-stained atrium. Dead escalators descend from readable dry upper floors into opaque black tidal water below. Broken storefronts, corroded rails and faded ordinary retail architecture establish that this was meant to be banal.

Nicole stands nearer the foreground rail, visibly drawn into the scale and human traces. Ryan is several steps back and oriented toward water level, exits and structure rather than wonder. Keep their acting natural and small against the building.

Across the upper levels, a handful of anonymous runners occupy the space with clipped work lights, noodles, wet socks, route maps and temporary gear. They should read as life without turning the mall into a festival.
The central hook is vertical: warm practical light and people above, black water below. The escalators visually connect the two and should remain legible at thumbnail size.
Reserve a clean upper band of fog-dark or shadowed architecture for masthead/trade dress; do not let signage or faces compete with it.
Palette: wet concrete gray, faded institutional green, deep cyan, black water, rust orange and a few sodium/contractor practical lights.
Spoiler ceiling: do not show the later building groan as structural collapse, the chapter's retreat, the Glass Rail, or any specific payoff after the mall becomes socially occupied.
directionInline: Pixel-read starsplitterrecords/StarSplitterVisions@main:sites/visions/public/images/covers/low-tide-signal-issue-01-cover.png before generation and carry forward only its cover masthead/trade-dress system. The Chapter 2 composition, character staging, environment, palette emphasis and selling hook come from this recipe.

Avoid horror-cover clichés: no ghosts, red emergency wash, looming monster shapes, haunted faces, or supernatural darkness. The unease comes from recognizable ordinary architecture becoming temporarily inhabited above real water.
Do not invent readable mall ads or promotional copy beyond incidental non-legible texture unless exact story canon requires it.

title: Cover — No Signal
summary: Sell Chapter 3 as social seduction: disconnection has become a feature. The cover should make the reader want to be on the Harbor Market roof with them even while the physical isolation remains obvious.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed portrait comic-cover image built around rooftop depth and the distant inland city.

Chris, Justin and Nicole occupy a rough roof edge or ventilation housing under a clipped contractor LED and headlamps. They are comfortable enough to look like friends hanging out rather than survivalists posing. Damp gear, cheap food or beer, and practical bags make the social space believable.
A phone or small device may sit dark in the lower foreground with a simple NO SIGNAL state if it can be rendered cleanly; it is a secondary clue, not the main object.
Beyond them: black water, drowned lower structures and deep fog, with Harbor Phase glowing far inland. The visual should make distance from ordinary life feel exhilarating before it feels dangerous.
Thumbnail read: three human silhouettes in a small island of practical light against a large dark cyan field and one distant warm city horizon.
Reserve upper sky/fog for the series masthead and a clean lower or upper-secondary zone for the chapter title. Keep lettering off faces and off the distant Harbor Phase glow.
Palette: deep cyan/black with practical white and small sodium amber; slightly richer social warmth than Chapters 1–2 without becoming neon nightlife.
Spoiler ceiling: do not show later reputation mechanics, escalation, commercialization, the group's cracks, or Ryan's withdrawal.
directionInline: Pixel-read starsplitterrecords/StarSplitterVisions@main:sites/visions/public/images/covers/low-tide-signal-issue-01-cover.png before generation for cover-only masthead/trade-dress continuity. Do not use preview-cover people as identity references; use approved character references when available.

The emotional promise is 'I want to be there' more than 'this is dangerous.' Keep the friends natural, loose and adult. No heroic skyline pose, influencer staging, nightclub neon, or cyberpunk roof aesthetic.
The cover should remain legible if the device text fails at thumbnail scale; the social island of light and faraway city are the primary read.

title: Cover — Between Runs
summary: Sell Chapter 4 as compulsion becoming routine. The offshore district is mostly absent from the image; its power is visible in how completely an ordinary inland apartment has reorganized itself around the next tide.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed portrait cover with a premium still-life/character composition rather than action spectacle.

Foreground: a packed contractor/tide bag, wet boots drying on a mat, charged headlamp, clipped tide monitor and rain shell already arranged beside Matt's apartment door. Everything looks used repeatedly, not freshly prepared for one adventure.

Matt is present deeper in the apartment, partly dressed for ordinary inland life or just home from work, but his body and eyeline are pulled toward the ready gear and door. Keep him human-scale; the bag is the visual anchor.

Through rain-lit windows or an open sightline deeper into the apartment, show normal comfortable Harbor Phase life continuing: warm interior light, transit outside, perhaps an unfinished meal or ordinary household clutter. The city works. The tension is what Matt keeps choosing anyway.
Thumbnail read: one dark packed bag/boot silhouette at the door, one practical headlamp/tide-device light, one human figure behind. The door becomes the compositional vector.
Reserve uncluttered wall/door-frame/upper window negative space for trade dress. Do not fill the cover with floating screens or montage fragments.
Palette: inland gray-blue and warm domestic practical light, invaded by the colder teal/white vocabulary of tide gear.
Spoiler ceiling: do not show Justin's later status, commercialization details, the full group crack, or Ryan's decision to pull away.
directionInline: Pixel-read starsplitterrecords/StarSplitterVisions@main:sites/visions/public/images/covers/low-tide-signal-issue-01-cover.png for exact cover masthead/trade-dress continuity only. This chapter cover should deliberately vary from the architecture-heavy earlier covers while still reading as the same series.

Make dependency visible through ordinary physical arrangement, not surreal imagery. No glowing tide symbols, giant clocks, dream overlays, split-screen memory effects, or metaphorical water inside the apartment.
Matt must not pose heroically. If his face is visible, anchor it to an approved Matt identity reference.

title: Cover — Return Tide
summary: Sell the Big Run as the season's dangerous perfect night. The route has opened farther and longer than usual, drawing confidence, crowds and ambition; one person looking back should be enough to make the apparent opportunity feel wrong.
settingText: Extreme low tide beyond the floodwall: the exposed route is unusually broad and extends far into fog toward the deep offshore district; many anonymous runners are entering under practical headlamps and vehicle/contractor light.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed portrait cover with the season's largest sense of scale. This is the one cover allowed to feel genuinely spectacular, but the spectacle must remain physically plausible and coastal.

Compose from slightly elevated behind the outgoing runners: an exceptionally broad exposed route cuts through black mud and shallow teal channels toward distant offshore structures. Dozens of anonymous headlamps spread outward, creating the impression of a rare event without becoming a concert or festival.

The six core friends are a recognizable cluster moving offshore. Ryan is slightly behind or offset, looking back/down toward water and route conditions while the others' body direction carries outward. Kevin may also be visually less celebratory. Do not arrange them as six equal poster poses.

The route should look safer than earlier crossings because it is wider and more exposed. A thin returning-water clue—small channels, sheen, or distant dark line—may exist at the margins, but do not depict the disaster or an obvious wall of water.
Thumbnail read: a bright fan of human lights across a huge dark route, one core cluster, one strong vanishing point into fog. The scale should immediately say THIS TIDE IS DIFFERENT.
Reserve upper fog/sky for masthead. Keep chapter-title placement away from the route vanishing point.
Palette: darkest black/cyan of the run with many practical whites and restrained sodium amber from the staging area; no lightning, no red danger wash, no supernatural storm glow.
Spoiler ceiling: do not show the failed return, stranded runners, Ryan disappearing, anyone injured, or the aftermath.
directionInline: Pixel-read starsplitterrecords/StarSplitterVisions@main:sites/visions/public/images/covers/low-tide-signal-issue-01-cover.png before generation for trade-dress continuity. Use approved character references for any core faces/bodies that are identifiable.

The selling contradiction is that the night looks unusually favorable. Do not telegraph the coming failure so loudly that the reader is told the answer; unease should come mainly from Ryan's attention and the scale of collective confidence.
No generic disaster-poster language, crashing waves, helicopters, emergency sirens, red strobes, or action-movie hero staging unless present in the issue recipe itself.

title: Cover — After the Water
summary: Sell Chapter 6 as aftermath becoming public story. The physical route is gone again; what remains inland is black water, attention, phones and people trying to turn consequence into a version they can share.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed portrait cover from the inland side of the floodwall after the route has vanished under black water.

Foreground/midground: wet barrier concrete, abandoned temporary runner lights or gear traces, rain sheen and a dark water horizon where the walking route used to be. The water should feel blank and indifferent, not violently active.

Along one side or behind the barrier, anonymous onlookers/media/runner spectators hold phones whose screens create a scattered cold glow. Keep screen content blurred or unreadable; the quantity of attention matters more than any specific post.

No identifiable core character is required. If distant figures are present, keep them small and non-countable so the cover does not resolve Ryan's status or turn the composition into a missing-person diagram.
Thumbnail read: one broad band of black water, one hard floodwall line, and a cluster of small phone lights pointed toward emptiness. The phones should look intrusive rather than futuristic.
Reserve fog/sky above the water for masthead and trade dress. Keep the chapter title in clean dark concrete or sky space.
Palette: cold gray-blue aftermath, black water, phone/device white-blue and minimal sodium reflections. Suppress the adventurous orange/rust energy of earlier offshore covers.
Spoiler ceiling: do not show Ryan's return, Chris deleting footage, Justin's later collapse, Matt's attempts to restore authority, or the chapter's final understanding.
directionInline: Pixel-read starsplitterrecords/StarSplitterVisions@main:sites/visions/public/images/covers/low-tide-signal-issue-01-cover.png for masthead/trade-dress continuity only. This cover should remain part of the same branded line while visually feeling stripped of the earlier adventure energy.
Do not use obituary, memorial, missing-person, candlelight, vigil, supernatural absence, or tragedy-poster clichés. The cover sells consequence and unwanted attention, not a predetermined death.
No readable social-media UI, hashtags, news chyron, or invented headlines.

title: Cover — The Last Low Tide
summary: Sell the finale as one last honest crossing after the mythology has burned off. The image should echo Chapter 1's threshold promise but remove the crowd, performance and mystery, making the same physical route feel newly sober.
panelPlan: Single full-bleed portrait finale cover with the sparsest composition of the series.

Dawn-blue flats stretch from foreground to fog. A narrow exposed service road or line of footprints leads offshore. A small, distant group of figures moves along it with ordinary gear and no surrounding crowd; keep them too small for face-level identification.

Harbor Phase is a dim but functioning presence far behind. The offshore district ahead is reduced to pale, ordinary geometry in fog rather than a dramatic looming mystery. Do not reveal the Deep District's specific schools, parks, clinics or residential details.
No one is performing for an audience. No phones held up. No runner gathering. No heroic leader silhouette. Body spacing should feel quieter and more deliberate than Chapter 1.
Thumbnail read: one pale dawn field, one dark road/footprint vector, one tiny group. The emptiness itself should be commercially distinctive after the denser middle-run covers.
Reserve large upper sky/fog area for masthead/trade dress; preserve generous breathing room around the chapter title.
Palette: dawn gray-blue, pale cyan, black mud, bone-white road fragments and almost no amber. The series should visually exhale.
Spoiler ceiling: do not show the Deep District revelation, specific ordinary civic spaces, the final conversation, who leads, or the final retreat inland.
directionInline: Pixel-read starsplitterrecords/StarSplitterVisions@main:sites/visions/public/images/covers/low-tide-signal-issue-01-cover.png before generation for the established Low Tide Signal cover trade dress. The finale should echo the compositional idea of Chapter 1—a crossing toward fog—without duplicating its camera, staging or emotional meaning.
The cover promise is not 'one last dangerous mission.' It is 'they still need to see it without the story they built around it.' Keep the image grounded, restrained and adult.
No sunset triumph, heroic reunion, memorial imagery, supernatural cleansing, or visual suggestion that the city or ocean has delivered a moral verdict.
